responsibilities: Own our data products end to end together with me: the datalake, the dashboards, the MCP for conversational analytics, the data API, and the analytics embedded in our product
Take a data need from the business and carry it the whole way, from getting new data into the datalake to the moment someone is using it to make a call
Build the transformation layer in SQL and dbt, and write the Python that moves data around and exposes it, from extraction jobs to API services
Keep the stack healthy and make it incrementally better: faster models, stronger data quality checks, less technical debt. You spot most of this yourself rather than waiting for it to be assigned
Turn data into a conclusion with an implication. Not a chart, but an answer a product or GTM team can act on: who isn't adopting, what drives adoption, what we should do differently
Present that work to product and go-to-market teams, and where it scales better, build them the tooling to answer their own questions
Work on larger initiatives that fundamentally change how our data stack works, alongside the day to day requests
Review my work the way I'll review yours

evidence.velocity_vs_rigour: Keep the stack healthy and make it incrementally better: faster models, stronger data quality checks, less technical debt.
evidence.velocity_vs_rigour_explanation: Quality language dominates with no shipping-speed vocabulary anywhere: the stack work is framed as "stronger data quality checks, less technical debt" and the candidate profile asks them to "go after root causes".
evidence.domain_risk: We embedded analytics into our EdTech product and built a data API for our users.
evidence.domain_risk_explanation: Errors would reach customer-facing analytics at "more than 200 universities in 28 countries", but the JD carries no financial, audit or regulatory language, so the stakes sit at business-decision level.
evidence.data_team_maturity: For the past year I've set up the Data function here.
evidence.data_team_maturity_explanation: The function exists and is growing past its founder — the datalake, dashboards and data API are already built and "the volume and complexity of it outgrows one person".
evidence.jd_authorship: Own our data products end to end together with me: the datalake, the dashboards, the MCP for conversational analytics, the data API, and the analytics embedded in our product
evidence.jd_authorship_explanation: Written in the first person by the Data Lead, naming each artefact the hire inherits, so a reader knows exactly what the job touches.
evidence.stakeholder_orientation: Present that work to product and go-to-market teams, and where it scales better, build them the tooling to answer their own questions
evidence.stakeholder_orientation_explanation: Product and commercial audiences are named together twice and carry equal weight — "an answer a product or GTM team can act on".
evidence.autonomy_level: Work on larger initiatives that fundamentally change how our data stack works, alongside the day to day requests
evidence.autonomy_level_explanation: Ownership of the stack sits next to request-driven delivery in the same bullet, the textbook mixed pattern.
evidence.ai_role_explanation: The hire owns an MCP server that exposes analytics to an AI assistant, so their output is what an AI system consumes; the separate expectation to "use AI tools like Claude Code or Codex" is the weaker of the two signals.
evidence.testing_framing_explanation: Data quality sits in the responsibilities as something the hire drives — "Keep the stack healthy and make it incrementally better" — not as a tool in a skills list.
evidence.loss_aversion_framing: You go after root causes. A small data anomaly bothers you until you understand why it's there
evidence.loss_aversion_framing_explanation: The fear named is a wrong number going unexplained, not regulatory exposure, and it sits behind delivery rather than ahead of it.
evidence.greenfield_vs_fix: So I'm hiring an Analytics Engineer for our HQ in Amsterdam to own and extend this with me.
evidence.greenfield_vs_fix_explanation: The stack already exists and the verbs split between extending it and paying down "technical debt", with new data products built on top.
evidence.loss_aversion: Reliability appears as stack hygiene rather than risk control: "Keep the stack healthy and make it incrementally better: faster models, stronger data quality checks, less technical debt."
